interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: DeepSWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Original, Long-Horizon Engineering Tasks
papers.authors: Wenqi Huang , Charley Lee , Leonard Tng , Serena Ge
papers.abstract: DeepSWE is a benchmark of 113 original, long-horizon software engineering tasks for evaluating coding agents. Most public agentic coding benchmarks follow SWE-bench in mining merged fixes from public GitHub repositories, which creates two problems: the fixes and their discussion were likely seen during pretraining, so a high score can reflect recall rather than problem-solving; and each task is graded by the tests that shipped with its merged fix, which were written to confirm one specific fix rather than grade an arbitrary solution, so they can fail a correct alternative or pass an incomplete one. DeepSWE avoids both. Its tasks are written from scratch across 91 active open-source repositories and five languages and are never contributed back upstream, so their reference solutions stay out of the public record that model training scrapes; and each task is graded by a hand-written verifier that checks the requested functionality and accepts any implementation that provides it. When an independent LLM judge re-reviews graded runs, it disagrees with DeepSWE's verifier about an order of magnitude less often than with SWE-Bench Pro's inherited tests (1.4% versus 32.4%). Despite being about half the length of SWE-Bench Pro's prompts, DeepSWE's prompts describe tasks whose reference solutions touch 5.5x more code, and the benchmark separates frontier agents across a wider score band than the leaderboards on which they otherwise cluster. We release the benchmark, its verifiers, and the full record of evaluation trajectories.
papers.Reasons for match: The paper introduces a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on original, long-horizon engineering tasks, which is relevant to LLM agents for scientific workflows.
papers.Short digest: The paper presents DeepSWE, a benchmark of 113 original software engineering tasks for evaluating coding agents, avoiding data contamination and test-set leakage. The main idea is to create tasks from scratch with hand-written verifiers, ensuring that solutions are not seen during pretraining and that grading is robust. This is relevant to astronomy because coding agents could be used for automated data analysis, literature review, and scientific workflows. A concrete workflow could be using a coding agent to write and debug code for JWST data reduction or spectral fitting. A limitation is that the benchmark focuses on software engineering, not scientific data analysis, so transferability to astronomy-specific tasks needs verification.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the benchmark tasks include any scientific or data-analysis-related coding
Look for the types of repositories and languages covered to assess relevance to astronomy tools
Examine the verifier design to see if it could be adapted for grading scientific code

papers.title: Agentic Neural Architecture Search
papers.authors: Seokhoon Jeong , Mijung Kim , Taehwan Kim
papers.abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) methods have grown increasingly efficient, yet they remain bounded by manually engineered search spaces that require substantial domain expertise and must be rebuilt for every new task. Large language models (LLMs) can generate architectures in an open-ended space, but how to optimally divide the labor between LLM-driven design and NAS-driven search remains unexplored. We propose a mechanism that bridges these two paradigms: an LLM produces a high-quality seed architecture, then decomposes it into a "slotted architecture", a scaffold with named, interchangeable module slots that automatically defines a bounded, task-specific search space for conventional NAS to explore, without manual engineering. We instantiate this mechanism in AgentNAS, a modular three-phase pipeline in which each component's contribution can be measured independently. On 17 tasks spanning classification, dense regression, segmentation, and multi-label tagging across diverse modalities (NAS-Bench-360 and Unseen NAS), AgentNAS establishes a new state of the art on 11 tasks, outperforming published baselines including task-specific expert designs. Ablation studies show that the two search mechanisms are broadly complementary: the LLM-generated seed already surpasses published baselines on the majority of tasks, and NAS delivers additional gains in most cases through combinatorial recombination across slots, a mode of search that independent LLM samples cannot replicate. These patterns hold across three LLMs of different capability levels, confirming that the division of labor is robust. Our code is available at this https URL .
papers.Reasons for match: The paper proposes an LLM-driven neural architecture search method, which is relevant to automated model design for astronomical data.
papers.Short digest: The paper introduces AgentNAS, a method that uses an LLM to generate a seed architecture and then decomposes it into a slotted architecture for conventional NAS to explore. It achieves state-of-the-art on 11 out of 17 tasks across diverse modalities. This is relevant to astronomy because it could automate the design of neural networks for tasks like galaxy morphology classification or spectral fitting. A concrete workflow could be using AgentNAS to design a custom architecture for classifying JWST images of high-redshift galaxies. A caveat is that the method requires significant computational resources and may need adaptation for astronomical data.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the types of tasks and modalities covered to assess relevance to astronomy
Look for the computational cost of the three-phase pipeline
Examine the slotted architecture design and its flexibility for different data types

papers.title: Playing ZendoWorld: Challenging AI Agents on Active Visual Concept Induction
papers.authors: Sophia Koehler , Antonia Wüst , Inga Ibs , Wasu Top Piriyakulkij , Wolfgang Stammer , Constantin Rothkopf , Kevin Ellis , Kristian Kersting
papers.subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
papers.abstract: A central challenge in building intelligent systems is enabling agents to jointly perceive complex inputs, form hypotheses about hidden patterns, and design informative experiments to test them. To study this problem, we propose ZendoWorld, a controlled interactive environment in which agents must infer a logical rule about visual game observations, acquire information by proposing new scenes, and refine their hypotheses based on feedback from the game environment. We evaluate several agents spanning pure VLM reasoning, Bayesian particle filtering, dynamic concept discovery, and neuro-symbolic methods. Our main findings are: (1) high accuracy in predicting labels for observed examples does not imply recovery of the underlying rule; (2) perception and induction are distinct bottlenecks for different agent classes; and (3) VLM-based agents propose near-uninformative experiments, failing to actively reduce hypothesis uncertainty. To compare these results, we collect human data on the task, which reveals a gap in inductive reasoning, particularly for more complex rules. Overall, ZENDOWORLD takes an important step toward evaluating intelligent agents and identifies concrete avenues for improvement, particularly in domains like scientific discovery.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly studies active concept induction in visual environments, relevant to scientific discovery agents.
papers.Short digest: This paper asks whether AI agents can actively infer hidden logical rules from visual observations by proposing informative experiments. The main result is that VLM-based agents propose near-uninformative experiments and fail to reduce hypothesis uncertainty, while neuro-symbolic methods perform better. This matters for astronomy because scientific discovery often requires designing experiments to test hypotheses about astronomical phenomena. The ZendoWorld environment provides a controlled testbed for evaluating agents' inductive reasoning and active learning capabilities. A limitation is that the visual concepts are simple geometric shapes, not complex astronomical data, so transfer to real astronomical workflows requires validation.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for the specific agent architectures compared and their performance on rule recovery vs. label prediction
Check whether the neuro-symbolic methods could be adapted to astronomical classification tasks
Examine the human baseline data to understand the gap between current AI and human inductive reasoning

papers.title: Beyond Thermal Imaging: Inferring Thermophysical Properties from Time-Resolved Thermal Observations
papers.authors: Chenghao Xu , Malcolm Mielle , Olga Fink
papers.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
papers.abstract: Inferring latent physical properties from sensory observations is a fundamental challenge in machine perception. Among available sensing modalities, thermal imaging is particularly promising because temperature evolution is directly governed by heat-transfer physics and therefore encodes information about underlying thermophysical properties of a scene. Recovering spatially resolved thermophysical properties from thermal observations could transform applications ranging from digital twins and infrastructure monitoring to robotics and scientific imaging. However, existing thermal scene reconstruction methods can recover temperature fields in complex 3D environments without identifying the thermophyiscal properties that govern thermal evolution, whereas inverse methods provide physically interpretable parameter estimation but typically rely on simplified geometries and controlled experimental conditions. Here we introduce ThermoField, a framework that unifies thermal scene reconstruction and thermophysical parameter estimation through differentiable heat-transfer simulation. The proposed framework represents these quantities as spatially varying neural fields and constrains them through scene geometry, governing heat-transfer physics, and temporal thermal observations. We demonstrate that ThermoField jointly reconstructs geometry, estimates spatially varying thermal diffusivity, and predicts thermal evolution under previously unseen environmental conditions. By integrating neural scene representations with differentiable heat-transfer solver, the framework enables physically interpretable parameter inference in complex 3D scenes. Our results establish a bridge between thermal scene reconstruction and inverse heat-transfer analysis, providing a unified approach for geometry reconstruction, thermophysical property estimation, and predictive thermal simulation from thermal observations.
papers.Reasons for match: The paper introduces a framework for inferring thermophysical properties from thermal observations, which is relevant to physical parameter estimation in astronomy.
papers.Short digest: The paper presents ThermoField, a framework that unifies thermal scene reconstruction and thermophysical parameter estimation through differentiable heat-transfer simulation. It uses neural fields to represent spatially varying properties and constrains them with physics. This is relevant to astronomy because similar inverse problems exist, e.g., inferring dust properties from infrared observations or modeling thermal emission from asteroids. A concrete workflow could be using this framework for analyzing JWST thermal infrared data of planetary surfaces or interstellar dust. A caveat is that the framework is designed for terrestrial thermal imaging, not astronomical observations, so adaptation to radiative transfer may be needed.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the differentiable heat-transfer simulation and its assumptions
Look for the neural field representation and its scalability to 3D scenes
Examine the evaluation on real-world thermal data and its relevance to astronomical observations

papers.title: Hallucination Self-Play: Bootstrapping Reinforced Detector via Evolved Generator
papers.authors: Shiping Yang , Shining Liang , Weihao Liu , Wenbiao Ding , Linjun Shou , Lu Cheng , Angel X. Chang
papers.abstract: Identifying faithfulness hallucinations in LLM-generated outputs remains challenging due to the scarcity of high-quality annotated data. Recent work relies on advanced LLMs to synthesize training data, including rationales, labels, and hallucinated claims. However, these methods treat the generator as a static component, limiting iterative improvement of the detector. To address this limitation, we introduce Hallucination Self-Play (HSP), a novel framework that enables the detector to bootstrap with an evolved generator. HSP involves two roles initialized from the same base model, a detector that assesses the faithfulness of model outputs, and a generator that produces increasingly hard-to-detect hallucinated responses. Specifically, the detector is first fine-tuned on human-labeled data and then employed as a reward model to train the generator via reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF). In turn, the evolved generator synthesizes hallucination data to further optimize the detector through rule-based reinforcement learning. Experiments on RAGTruth benchmark and two model families demonstrate that the proposed framework can progressively enhance a small LLM to match or even outperform advanced LLMs without external supervision. Our code is available at this https URL .
papers.Reasons for match: The paper addresses hallucination detection in LLMs, which is relevant for trustworthy AI in scientific workflows, but the method is NLP-focused and not astronomy-specific.
papers.Short digest: The paper aims to improve detection of faithfulness hallucinations in LLM outputs, where the model generates factually incorrect or unsupported statements. The main idea is Hallucination Self-Play (HSP), a framework where a detector and generator are iteratively trained: the detector is first fine-tuned on human data, then used as a reward model to train a generator via reinforcement learning from AI feedback to produce harder-to-detect hallucinations; the evolved generator then synthesizes data to further improve the detector. For astronomy, this could help build more reliable LLM-based tools for literature review or data analysis by reducing hallucinated claims. A concrete workflow could be using HSP to train a detector that flags unsupported statements in LLM-generated summaries of JWST papers or catalogs. A key caveat is that the method is demonstrated on a general RAG benchmark, not on scientific or astronomical data, so domain adaptation and evaluation would be needed.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the method is evaluated on scientific or domain-specific data, or only on general NLP benchmarks.
Look for analysis of the types of hallucinations the detector catches (e.g., factual vs. reasoning errors) and whether they apply to astronomy contexts.
